title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
This exercise brings together two foundations of geospatial analysis in R: preparing spatial data correctly and communicating a demographic pattern with a choropleth map.
The workflow is based on the assigned geospatial data wrangling and choropleth mapping chapters. The code below is written as my own working template and will be updated with outputs after the data has been downloaded and run in RStudio.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Getting started
The analysis uses sf for vector operations, tidyverse for data wrangling and charts, and tmap for thematic mapping.
pacman::p_load(
  sf,
  tidyverse,
  tmap,
  units
)

tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Part 1: Geospatial data wrangling

Import the spatial layers
GeoJSON can be read directly with st_read(). I standardise the three layers to SVY21 so that distances and areas are measured in metres.
mpsz14 <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

preschools <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/PreSchoolsLocation.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

cycling_paths <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/CyclingPathNetwork.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)


Inspect before analysing
I check the feature count, geometry type and CRS immediately after import. This catches missing projections and unexpected geometry before they affect later calculations.
spatial_check <- tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Pre-schools", "Cycling paths"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz14), nrow(preschools), nrow(cycling_paths)),
  geometry = c(
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(mpsz14)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(preschools)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(cycling_paths)), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz14)$epsg, st_crs(preschools)$epsg, st_crs(cycling_paths)$epsg)
)

spatial_check
plot(st_geometry(mpsz14), col = "grey95", border = "white")
plot(st_geometry(cycling_paths), col = "#39735f", add = TRUE)
plot(st_geometry(preschools), col = "#d85b3f", pch = 16, cex = 0.25, add = TRUE)






NoteCRS check



st_set_crs() labels coordinates when the existing label is missing or wrong; it does not move the features. st_transform() recalculates coordinates in another reference system. For distance and area work in Singapore, I use EPSG:3414.




Convert Airbnb records to spatial points
The Airbnb file is tabular, but its longitude and latitude columns allow it to be converted to an sf object. The coordinates begin in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) and are then transformed to SVY21.
listings <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/listings.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

listings_sf <- listings |>
  drop_na(longitude, latitude) |>
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
    crs = 4326,
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  st_transform(3414)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz14, fill = "grey96", colour = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = listings_sf, colour = "#d85b3f", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.45) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Airbnb listings in Singapore",
    subtitle = "Point locations over Master Plan 2014 subzones"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


Estimate land around cycling paths
A five-metre buffer represents the reserved strip on both sides of each path. I dissolve the lines before buffering so overlapping segments are not counted more than once.
cycling_buffer <- cycling_paths |>
  st_geometry() |>
  st_union() |>
  st_buffer(dist = 5)

cycling_buffer_area <- cycling_buffer |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units(ha)

cycling_buffer_area
The result should be interpreted as an indicative planimetric area. It does not account for parcel ownership, terrain or construction constraints.


Count pre-schools by subzone
For each subzone, st_intersects() returns the pre-school points that fall within it. I convert the list of matches to a count and divide by area to obtain a comparable density.
mpsz14_summary <- mpsz14 |>
  mutate(
    preschool_count = lengths(st_intersects(mpsz14, preschools)),
    area_km2 = as.numeric(set_units(st_area(geometry), km^2)),
    preschool_density = preschool_count / area_km2
  )
mpsz14_summary |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(preschool_count)) |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, preschool_count, area_km2, preschool_density) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)


Explore the distribution
ggplot(mpsz14_summary, aes(x = preschool_count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, colour = "white", fill = "#39735f") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of pre-schools across subzones",
    x = "Number of pre-schools",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(mpsz14_summary, aes(x = area_km2, y = preschool_count)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#d85b3f", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#17333d") +
  labs(
    title = "Subzone area and number of pre-schools",
    x = "Subzone area (km²)",
    y = "Number of pre-schools"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
When the code is run, I will comment on the skewness of the count distribution, any unusually high values and whether larger subzones consistently contain more pre-schools. The density measure should be read alongside counts because a small subzone can have a high density without having many facilities.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Part 2: Choropleth mapping

Prepare population data
The goal is to map the dependency ratio by planning subzone:
\[
\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\text{young population} + \text{aged population}}{\text{economically active population}}
\]
I extract the starting age from each label, classify the rows into three population bands, and then aggregate male and female records. This avoids relying on the position of columns after reshaping.
popdata <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

popdata2024 <- popdata |>
  mutate(
    age_start = parse_number(AG),
    age_band = case_when(
      between(age_start, 0, 24) ~ "YOUNG",
      between(age_start, 25, 64) ~ "ECONOMY ACTIVE",
      age_start >= 65 ~ "AGED",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(age_band)) |>
  group_by(PA, SZ, age_band) |>
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = age_band, values_from = POP, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(
    TOTAL = YOUNG + `ECONOMY ACTIVE` + AGED,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`,
    PA = str_to_upper(PA),
    SZ = str_to_upper(SZ)
  ) |>
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0) |>
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)






WarningCheck the age labels



Run unique(popdata$AG) before aggregation. The code assumes each age label begins with its lower bound, such as 0-4 or 65-69; any total row is excluded because it has no starting age.




Join population to subzones
mpsz19 <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

mpsz_pop2024 <- mpsz19 |>
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(SUBZONE_N)) |>
  left_join(popdata2024, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

join_check <- mpsz_pop2024 |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    subzones = n(),
    matched = sum(!is.na(DEPENDENCY)),
    unmatched = sum(is.na(DEPENDENCY))
  )

join_check
The join check is important: unmatched subzones may be non-residential, but they can also reveal spelling or naming differences that require investigation.


Compare classification methods
A choropleth is shaped by its class boundaries. The following small multiples keep the number of classes fixed while comparing equal intervals, quantiles and Jenks natural breaks.
map_equal <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Equal interval")
  )

map_quantile <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Quantile")
  )

map_jenks <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Jenks")
  )

tmap_arrange(map_equal, map_quantile, map_jenks, ncol = 3)
Equal intervals make the legend easy to compare, quantiles balance the number of subzones in each class, and Jenks emphasises clusters in the observed distribution. I will choose the method that best supports comparison without hiding unusually high or low ratios.


Final map
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "jenks",
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.4
  ) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio by Singapore planning subzone, 2024") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_credits(
    "Sources: URA Master Plan 2019 and Singapore Department of Statistics",
    position = c("left", "bottom")
  ) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Reflection
The main lesson is that a map is only the final stage of a longer workflow. Geometry validity, CRS choice, grouping rules and join quality all affect the result before colours are assigned. I should therefore report these checks together with the map and avoid treating a high dependency ratio as a complete explanation of local needs.
